english_text: It was pretty good back then. Based on what I know that I say it was good back then. People were important to one another, enjoyed [one] another, had humorous conversations. But, as time went on, I began to see it change. The value of things made it hard for us—on the price of things, about money. But as far as the mind and the way of thinking, it was better than the value of anything. But, nowadays, the price of things is really hard on us. The reason is people have moved from the way that they believed. And how man should walk here on this earth, with his own strength, and gather good to prosper. The way I see it, their own eyes have blinded them, Charlie. That’s what I see. As well as belief—they don’t believe anymore. They have nothing to do with the way we did things in the past. As far as I know, it is going to go back to that. Two different things are going to happen. I tell people, “It’s just going to be the way we are living now.” And, the other thing, is it going to be the way it was? And the way a person wants to be, and wants to live, he will choose. It will be good, or it will be sad. And it is sad, like I am saying, the things that are happening in the world is blinding the people. They are drawn to that. And the Lord that we have been provided is very joyful they are letting go of that. They feel like there is no truth. Quickly, they will think something else. That was the way it was. We were fishing, this One sitting here, I believe you know, too? But I don’t know if he knows where this is at? Do you know where Hickory Hollow is? Where the cemetery is? ‘Hickory Van Hollow’ they call it. Where the cemetery is, on the edge of the field, on this side, is where we used to live. In 1960 we had a drought. Charlie, where I am saying, I traveled that far through this field to the big Sallisaw Creek. A man named Man Hitter owned those fields. I would go across there with two buckets. There was a well there, on the creek. But in the creek there was no water—it was dry. That’s what happened. Then I done as much as could do, bending about to bring them water before it got hot. That’s the way it was when I grew up. And they washed... Back then washers did not exist. They call them ‘washing machine’ in English, they didn’t exist then. That far in the hollow, we were coming from there. They had one of those big things you put water in. They would take it that far to the big creek. I was telling this One, we are the same age, there is a rock there that has a groove in it. A hard rock there. I saw Mom for the first time, doing this. I was watching her I said, “Mom why are you beating those rocks? You are going to put holes in there.” I told her—we probably had one change of clothes. There was a rock there this big, ’kinda round. We were putting water in there for her, and she would put them [clothes] in there. And for soap—she was using that hard soap, all that. And, when she got enough, she pound them with the rocks. That’s when I thought she was going to put holes in our clothes. And, then we would help wring them out, just there on the creek, we hung clothes on the branches. While the clothes were drying we would look for our food. Crawdads, fish, and we would stick our hands under rocks. Yeah, we would just cook right there. Sometimes they would have potatoes. About this time there would be a garden, things like that, as well as onion. They would have a pan in the fire. They would boil crawdads in there. They would fry those crawdads. When they would get done, and when they were almost done, they would put the potatoes and onions, and those ‘kian’ they call them. Them elders always had those kian, hot peppers. They would cut those up. That was a good soup to drink. And crawdads fried real soft. Yeah that’s the way it was. I know they would, still won’t, feel like doing it [the laundry]—that’s the way it is. In the winter, we would cut wood to build a fire.

english_text: We loaded them up. First it was for the cook stove. And, Charlie if you remember—horse pulled wagon, where they hook up was all sticking out in the back. And that’s what it was in 1958. That’s the way it was back then. Also, you could cut wood wherever. Nobody would say nothing. Nobody would come and see you. There, where I am talking about, I would help my dad make fence posts and railroad ties. We would cut them down, so he could make posts and ties. I tell my family I have grown up. Boy, I worked hard since I was six years old. I was six years old, Charlie—I started then. But that’s the way it was then. A child wasn’t going to lay down somewhere, or be sitting somewhere, in the cold, in the heat. Where Charlie lives, we would be that far [away] on that mountain, we would come from out of that hollow. We would leave there at four in the morning. There, past where y’all live, in that corner where that gate is, we would be walking right there. It would turn daylight. We would get there—it is called ‘Two Springs.’ On the other ridge, that’s where it was. We would be coming back in the evening. We would get back to the hollow around nine the next morning. The same thing, that’s the way it was back then. That’s the kind of things he would do. He [Dad] bought that land where we live now. He paid it off, he borrowed money from the Cherokee Nation.

Boy, I worked hard since I was six years old. I was six years old, Charlie—I started then. But that’s the way it was then. How old was you then, this time you’re talking about?

Me, I was maybe around eight years old. They opened it up. A soldier, clothes, a soldier stepped down. I thought he was the one that helps people. I was watching him. Everyone was standing where the door is. They let him out, then they went back that way, and there they let out two dogs—bluetick hound dogs. That was him, Fish, I never knew then. Just the next morning they left. There was a White man that lived on the mountain, Michael, this side—Jim Harris. They went after those horses and wagon, he bought two pairs. We were all up there where Fish grew up. It was late in the afternoon. I heard the sound of chains. I was looking that way, I was at the creek looking for crawdads, I seen somethings—ears they were this long [gestures]. I thought, “What is that?” It was them, those mules and a plow. They had all those things in there, and they were leading two cows for milking, and in the other wagon, ducks, chickens. They had it full in there. It started there, it was probably past noon when they came. When they untied the horses, they hooked up the turning plows. It started then, it didn’t start in the morning, it started then. That’s what I tell these living, that are my family. Boy, I miss them old ones. I miss them, there wasn’t no time for them. It didn’t matter what time. It could be midnight, if they say, “Let’s do it, let’s do it.” They was going to do it. That’s the way them elders were, they were all like that, not just certain ones. They were all like that. The last, where his mom lived down in the hollow, there is a few times that I know of, “Let’s kill a hog, it will just take us a little while. It won’t be long we will be eating fresh meat.” I know of one time, no I know of three times, it was towards midnight we killed a hog. Tsukiyasgi built a fire. He said, “It won’t take long to boil water.” We went and killed it, the water was boiling, then we scraped it, and gutted it. In just a little while we were eating meat and gravy.
